one_liner: Header-only C++20 async logger: lock-free ring, formatting deferred to a writer thread; 2-5x spdlog async on producer-side throughput.
what_it_does: slick-logger is a header-only C++20 logging library with spdlog-like LOG_INFO/LOG_DEBUG macros and std::format-style placeholders. A singleton Logger is set up with init(queue_size), owns console, file, rotating, daily and binary sinks, and drains entries on one background writer thread. It also has spdlog-style pattern flags, source locations by default, per-sink logging, runtime statistics, and a shared-memory multi-process mode in which producer processes write into a segment that one collector process drains. The interface is not a drop-in for spdlog's logger objects.
how_it_is_fast: The calling thread only stamps the entry (timestamp, thread id, source location) and copies the arguments into a slot of a lock-free MPMC ring (slick-queue), claimed with one CAS on a shared counter. String-literal format strings are stored as pointers, and dynamic strings are copied into a separate string ring in 64-byte (cache-line) units so producers do not false-share. All std::format work and sink I/O happens later on the writer thread, which flushes once per drained batch rather than per line. Pattern rendering uses pre-parsed op lists and a per-second cached broken-down time.
when_to_use: Latency-sensitive threads (trading, game loops, real-time services) where a log call should cost about 100-350 ns on the producer and never wait on disk.
Many producer threads logging at once: in the author's scaling harness total enqueue throughput kept rising up to 16 threads, while spdlog_async fell.
Several processes on one host that should write to one log through a shared-memory collector.
C++20 code bases that already use std::format and want spdlog-like patterns and sinks without depending on fmt.
when_not_to_use: When every log line must be kept: both rings are lossy and have no backpressure, so producers that outrun the writer overwrite older entries (a loss counter exists only with SLICK_LOGGER_ENABLE_LOSS_DETECTION).
Toolchains without C++20 std::format (needs GCC 11+, Clang 14+ or MSVC 19.29+).
Code that passes const char array members or locals as the format string: the literal-detection heuristic stores only a pointer, which can dangle before the writer reads it.
Projects that need a mature, widely deployed logger: 5 stars, 2 forks, single-vendor project.
Custom formatter types passed through a pre-built std::format_args: they are logged as <handle>.

integration.min_toolchain: C++20 with std::format: GCC 11+, Clang 14+, MSVC 19.29+; CMake 3.20+
integration.thread_safety: Safe for concurrent LOG_* calls from any thread; sinks are touched only by the single writer thread; set_instance() must be called before plugin threads log.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: macros and pattern flags resemble spdlog, but it uses a global Logger singleton with its own sink classes instead of spdlog logger objects, and its queue drops entries where spdlog_async blocks by default.

gotchas: Lossy rings: messages are dropped silently on overrun unless loss detection is compiled in. The thread-scaling table (9.36M vs 114K ops/s at 16 threads) pushes 100,000 messages per thread through a 65,536-entry ring, so slick-logger can overwrite entries while spdlog_async (default block policy) waits for its writer. That row compares lossy enqueue with lossless delivery.

Throughput figures stop the timer when producers return; the writer's drain and flush are outside the timed region for both async loggers. The main suite's 50,000 messages fit in a 65,536-slot queue, so it measures enqueue cost and not sustained throughput.

Each header-only binary (exe, .dll/.so) gets its own Logger unless you share it with Logger::set_instance(), and the host must flush() before dlclose/FreeLibrary because queued entries point at the plugin's string literals.
Raising a sink's min_level also drops entries that are already queued; on POSIX, shared-memory segments are never shm_unlink'ed, so cleanup is manual.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Quill or fmtlog when you want std::format with no fmt dependency, Windows and MSVC as first-class targets, and a built-in multi-process shared-memory collector. Quill, NanoLog and XTR have far wider use and independent latency tables (Quill's harness), so prefer them when maturity or guaranteed delivery (Quill's blocking queue option) matters more.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's suite (benchmarks/benchmark_main.cpp; MSVC 19.44 /O2 C++20, Ryzen 9 5900HX, Windows 11, local NVMe; 50,000 messages x 3 runs), producer-side throughput for literal-only messages was 7.67M ops/s against spdlog 1.12.0 async 3.77M and sync 1.30M at 1 thread, and 10.96M against 1.93M and 0.49M at 8 threads; for three-argument messages it was 4.75M against 0.90M (async) at 1 thread. Both async loggers used 65,536-slot queues and were timed until the producers returned; the README table says spdlog_async used an 8,192-slot queue, but the code uses 65,536.
status_note: Actively maintained (v2.2.0 released 2026-09-28) and MIT-licensed, so copyable; adoption is very low (5 stars) and all numbers are first-party, from one Windows laptop.
